content.description: Mental illness accounts for **20% of illness worldwide**, but gets only 2% of health budgets. Here is why a cause left aside for so long is becoming a major social issue.

hero.hook: One in five illnesses worldwide affects the mind, yet mental health gets barely 2% of health budgets.

blocks.text: Long pushed aside by medicine, mental health is becoming one of the great challenges of the 21st century. It is not just the absence of psychiatric disorders: it is a state of well-being that lets a person use their potential and cope with the difficulties of life.
A striking paradox remains: these disorders make up about 20% of illness worldwide, but receive only 2% of health budgets. This course digs into the roots of that silent crisis.

**Depression** is now the leading cause of disability in the world, ahead of heart disease and diabetes. Marked by lasting sadness and a loss of interest in everything, it reaches every group in the population, yet stays under-diagnosed in many parts of the world.

blocks.caption: Depression is now the leading cause of disability worldwide

blocks.text: Generalized anxiety affects about 300 million people worldwide. That suffering sometimes leads to suicide, which causes 700,000 deaths a year, more than wars and natural disasters combined.
The word “melancholy” comes from ancient Greek and means literally “black bile.” In antiquity, people believed depression was caused by too much of that fluid in the body.

In 2019, the World Health Organization took a symbolic step by recognizing [[Burnout (occupational exhaustion)]] as a work-related phenomenon. The move shifts responsibility away from the individual alone and toward the workplace itself.

Every age group is affected, but teenagers and young adults are the biggest worry. In the United States, anxiety and depression among people aged 12 to 25 nearly doubled in a decade, with a clear turning point around 2012.

blocks.caption: The explosion of social media lines up with a sharp rise in anxiety among the young

blocks.text: That date matches the moment smartphones and social media became universal. The psychologist Jean Twenge argues that the change upended how young people socialize: [[Upward social comparison]], where you measure yourself against unrealistic standards of living, creates a deep sense of never being enough.

Add [[Cyber-victimization]] and the lack of sleep caused by screen light. Social media runs on loops of [[Dopaminergic reinforcement]] that can turn addictive and pull young people away from sport and from real rest.

Mental health is not only a private matter: it hits productivity directly. Burnout and distress at work are estimated to cost 300 billion dollars a year in the United States alone, counting absences, constant turnover, and employees who show up but cannot work well.

blocks.caption: The cost of burnout runs into hundreds of billions of dollars every year

blocks.text: Faced with that bill, companies are building prevention programs, but the challenge is nowhere near solved in poor countries, where seeing a psychiatrist is almost impossible. One of the strongest levers is still destigmatization: when a public figure like the athlete Simone Biles speaks openly about her struggles, she helps turn a source of shame into a real health question.

The future of mental health depends on our ability to move from medicine that treats a crisis once it arrives to an approach that prevents it. That means rethinking city planning, school and the rhythm of work, to cut sources of stress before they do damage.
New paths are opening, such as digital therapies and artificial intelligence, to make up for the shortage of practitioners, though these tools also raise questions about the privacy of personal data.

Mental health is also tied to today's big crises: the idea of eco-anxiety shows how global threats like the climate reach straight into our psychological balance. Treating mental health as an essential pillar of society is becoming a condition for facing the crises ahead.

Mental health accounts for 20% of illness worldwide but only 2% of health budgets. Between depression, burnout and the effect of screens on the young, it is becoming a social issue as urgent as it is economic.

Artificial intelligence.explanation: Used here to refer to algorithms and conversational agents (chatbots) capable of performing a first level of psychiatric monitoring or sorting.

Burn-out.explanation: Chronic exhaustion syndrome caused by overwork, recognized by the WHO since 2019 as an occupational phenomenon. It is characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a reduced sense of accomplishment.

Burnout.explanation: A syndrome of chronic exhaustion caused by overwork, recognized by the WHO since 2019 as an occupational phenomenon. It is characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a reduced sense of accomplishment.

Burnout (occupational exhaustion).explanation: A syndrome of chronic exhaustion caused by overwork, recognized by the WHO since 2019 as an occupational phenomenon. It is characterized by emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and a reduced sense of accomplishment.

Cyber-victimization.explanation: Form of harassment occurring via digital tools, including insults, the spreading of rumors, or online social exclusion.

Dopaminergic reinforcement.explanation: Biological mechanism linked to the reward circuit in the brain, stimulated by notifications and 'likes' on social media, which can lead to addiction.

Eco-anxiety.explanation: Form of psychic distress linked to the feeling of helplessness in the face of climate change and future environmental threats.

Haidt.explanation: Psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues that the massive adoption of smartphones by adolescents starting in 2012 is the primary cause of the epidemic of depression and anxiety among young people. The scientific debate remains intense.

Simone Biles.explanation: Multi-medalist American gymnast who, by withdrawing from several events at the Tokyo 2021 Olympics to preserve her mental health, sparked a global debate on the subject.

Smartphones and mental health hypothesis.explanation: Psychologist Jonathan Haidt argues that the massive adoption of smartphones by adolescents starting in 2012 is the primary cause of the epidemic of depression and anxiety among young people. The scientific debate remains intense.
